segments.english: She said to him, "Also straw, also fodder, plenty with us, also room to lodge."
segments.literal: and-said she to-him also straw also fodder much with-us also place to-lodge

tokens.note: wayyiqtol; the answer follows the question at once

phrases.literal: 'and-said she to-him': the wayyiqtol continues the answer
'also straw': the first of four gam, each set before its item
'much with-us': a verbless clause, kept verbless in the English
'also place to-lodge': the last item, a place to spend the night

grammar: וַתֹּאמֶר אֵלָיו is a wayyiqtol: the answer comes straight after the question, with no new subject named.
Four גַּם stand in the answer, each before its own item (straw, fodder, room); the English keeps all four so that the list reads as the Hebrew gives it.
רַב עִמָּנוּ has no verb; the English keeps it verbless as "plenty with us".
The etnaḥta on עִמָּנוּ divides the answer: the feed for the animals before it, the room for the night after it.
segments.note: The answer gives feed and room, more than a yes or no. Radak's reading that she answered beyond the question is recorded in the commentary, not in the English.

commentary.summary: Rashi: every food of the camels is called מִסְפּוֹא, such as straw and barley.
Radak: she answered more than he asked, to show that she was generous of heart.
Radak: מִסְפּוֹא is the general word for beasts' food other than straw, that is barley and foxtail.
Radak: the repeated גַּם is the idiom of the language, each item adding to the one before.
Sforno: the גַּם is not only a place for the camels; there is also straw and fodder to feed them.
Sforno: the room is for you and your men.

segments.english: The man bowed down and prostrated himself to the LORD.

tokens.note: wayyiqtol; the first of two acts
hitpaʿel, reflexive: he bows himself to the ground

phrases.literal: 'and-bowed the-man': the first act, a wayyiqtol
'to the-LORD': the one worshipped, with ל

grammar: Two wayyiqtol verbs in sequence: the man first bows down (קָדַד), then prostrates himself (שָׁחָה).
הִשְׁתַּחֲוָיָה is the hitpaʿel of שָׁחָה; the form is reflexive, so the English has "himself".
The ל of לַיהוָה marks the one worshipped; the English keeps "to" as the Hebrew has it.
The munaḥ on וַיִּקֹּד, the tipḥa on וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ and the silluq on the name divide the verse into its two acts and the name.

commentary.summary: Radak: הִשְׁתַּחֲוָיָה is more than קִידָה; the sages say קִידָה is bowing on the face and הִשְׁתַּחֲוָיָה is spreading out the hands and feet. He thanked God that his way succeeded.

apparatus: 24:26.4 vowels: WLC reads לַֽיהוָֽה; the base text reads לַֽיהֹוָֽה׃ (the same name, differently pointed).

segments.english: He said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of my lord Abraham, who has not forsaken his kindness and his faithfulness from my lord; as for me, on the way the LORD led me to the house of my lord's brothers."
segments.literal: and-said blessed the-LORD God-of my-lord Abraham who not forsook his-kindness and-his-faithfulness from-with my-lord; I on-the-way led-me the-LORD house brothers-of my-lord

tokens.note: wayyiqtol; the speech that follows is his
qal passive participle used as a predicate; the Hebrew has no verb, so "be" is the English copula
construct with suffix: "my lord", the title of a man
ב with the article: the way he was on
lexicon sense 2: a brother in the wider sense of a relative

phrases.literal: 'blessed': the participle, the Hebrew has no verb
'who not forsook': a relative clause with a negated qatal

phrases.english: and his faithfulness from my lord

phrases.literal: 'I': the pronoun opens the second clause

phrases.english: on the way the LORD led me
to the house of my lord's brothers
phrases.literal: 'house brothers-of my-lord': a construct chain; the English adds 'to' for the verb of leading

grammar: בָּרוּךְ יְהוָה has no verb: the participle is a predicate, and the English "Blessed be" supplies the copula that the form needs. It is the one copula this translation adds.
אֲשֶׁר לֹא־עָזַב is a relative clause with a negated qatal: "who has not forsaken" reports a completed act.
חַסְדּוֹ וַאֲמִתּוֹ is a pair of nouns, חֶסֶד and אֱמֶת, each with its own suffix; the pair recurs in the Hebrew Bible for steady loyalty and reliability.
בַּדֶּרֶךְ: the ב carries the article, so the word is "on the way" he was on; Rashi reads it as the road he needed.
The etnaḥta on אֲדֹנִי divides the speech: the blessing before it, the account of the journey after it.
segments.note: The English supplies "be" in the first clause; see the grammar note. Otherwise the speech keeps the Hebrew's order and its verbless clauses.

commentary.summary: Rashi: דֶּרֶךְ here is the known, straight road, the one he needed; the ב with patah marks a matter already known.
Radak: for one who pursues good, the good God owes him provision, which is emet; ḥesed is the surplus of good, and that is why he found him a wife from his father's house.
Radak: he did not know where he would lodge.
Radak: the plural אֲחֵי and the singular "daughter of my brother" in verse 48 refer to the same matter.

segments.english: The girl ran and told her mother's household in these words.
segments.literal: and-ran the-girl and-told to-house mother-her like-the-words these

tokens.note: lexicon sense 5: the house as the family that lives in it
כְּ gives a likeness, not an identity: the report is in the manner of these words

phrases.literal: 'and-ran the-girl': two wayyiqtol-led clauses in one
'like-the-words these': a likeness of the words, not a verbatim report

grammar: וַתָּרָץ and וַתַּגֵּד are two wayyiqtol verbs in sequence: she ran, then she told.
לְבֵית אִמָּהּ, "the house of her mother", is the household; the English uses "household" for the family.
כַּדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה gives a likeness: she reported in the manner of these words, which may differ in detail.
The munaḥ on לְבֵית and the tipḥa on כַּדְּבָרִים mark the report and its closing words; the silluq on הָאֵלֶּה ends the verse.

commentary.summary: Rashi: women had a house in which to sit at their work, and a daughter reports only to her mother.
Radak: she ran to the house with joy.
Radak: the daughter's stories and talk are with her mother, not with her father.
Radak: "as these words" allows for less, more, or different wording; that is the manner of the narrator.

segments.english: And to Rebekah a brother, his name Laban; and Laban ran to the man outside, to the spring.
segments.literal: and-to-Rebekah brother, and-his-name Laban; and-ran Laban to-the-man outside to-the-spring

phrases.literal: 'and-ran Laban': the wayyiqtol returns to the action

grammar: The first two clauses, וּלְרִבְקָה אָח and וּשְׁמוֹ לָבָן, have no verb; the English keeps them verbless.
וַיָּרָץ returns the narrative to action after the two clauses.
The ה on חוּצָה is directional: the man is outside, and Laban runs to him at the spring.
The etnaḥta on לָבָן divides the two clauses about Laban from the action; the silluq on הָעָיִן ends the verse.
segments.note: Both clauses are verbless in the Hebrew, and the English keeps them verbless. The reading "brother" as a relative is supported by Radak's comment.

commentary.summary: Rashi asks why Laban ran and for what purpose he ran.
Radak: since he is not written in the genealogy of Nahor, the text calls him "brother".
Sforno: Laban ran to see a rich guest who had come to the city, not to bring him into his house.

segments.english: When he saw the ring and the bracelets on his sister's hands, and when he heard the words of Rebekah his sister, saying, "Thus the man spoke to me," he came to the man; and look, standing by the camels at the spring.
segments.literal: and-it-was as-seeing (object) the-ring and-(object) the-bracelets upon-hands-of his-sister, and-as-hearing (object) words-of Rebekah his-sister saying: thus spoke to-me the-man; and-came to-the-man, and-look standing upon the-camels upon the-spring

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of היה with a temporal infinitive; "it was" is not rendered
participle; its subject is the man, the traveller with the camels

phrases.english: the words of Rebekah his sister
Thus the man spoke to me
phrases.literal: 'thus spoke to-me the-man': the report, in her words

phrases.english: standing by the camels at the spring

grammar: וַיְהִי כִּרְאֹת is "when he saw": the wayehi with a temporal infinitive; the English does not render "it was".
The two object markers אֵת before הַנֶּזֶם and הַצְּמִדִים are not rendered; the English has "the ring and the bracelets".
The second clause, וּכְשָׁמְעוֹ, repeats the first: "and when he heard" the words of Rebekah.
לֵאמֹר introduces Rebekah's words, which are quoted inside the narrative; the speech closes before "he came".
The etnaḥta on הָאִישׁ (24:30.19) divides the two clauses; the silluq on הָעָיִן ends the verse with the scene.
segments.note: The sentence is long because the Hebrew is: when he saw, when he heard, he came, and look. The English keeps that order. The subject of עֹמֵד is the man, not Laban.
context: The נֶזֶם is a jewel worn at the nose or the ear; this verse does not say which, so the English keeps the general word "ring".

commentary.summary: Rashi: Laban said, "this one is rich," and fixed his eyes on the money.
Rashi: he stood over the camels to guard them, as in 18:8, that is, to attend to them.
Radak: Laban was grudging with his sister; when he saw the ring and the bracelets he ran to bring the man home.
Radak: it seems the man spoke to her about coming to the city to take a wife for his master's son.
Radak: he stood waiting, expecting the girl, her father or her brother to come back and bring him in.
Sforno: Laban thought it not fitting to be ungrateful for the gift.
Sforno: Eliezer asked her whether her father's house had room for them to lodge.
Sforno: Laban came to the man to bring him into his house.
Sforno: he stood by the camels to look after their needs, not expecting to lodge in the house until word came from the man.

segments.english: He said, "Come in, blessed of the LORD! Why do you stand outside? Now I have cleared the house and a place for the camels."
segments.literal: and-said come blessed the-LORD why you-will-stand outside and-I cleared the-house and-place for-the-camels

tokens.note: qal passive participle; "blessed of the LORD"
לָמָּה: why, the interrogative with ל
yiqtol, 2ms: the present form in a question
piʿel perfect 1cs; the lexicon entry for פָּנָה lists no piʿel sense, so no sense is given; "cleared" is from the context

phrases.literal: 'come': the imperative, with 'in' for the lexicon sense

phrases.english: Now I have cleared the house and a place for the camels

grammar: בּוֹא בְּרוּךְ is an imperative with a participle: "come in, blessed of the LORD".
לָמָּה is "why": the interrogative מָה with the preposition ל.
תַעֲמֹד is a yiqtol, 2ms; "do you stand" is the English form for a question in the present.
פִּנִּיתִי is a piʿel perfect; the lexicon has no piʿel sense, so the English "cleared" comes from the sense of the clause.
The zaqef gadol on וַיֹּאמֶר marks the speech; the etnaḥta on יְהוָה divides the blessing from the question; the silluq on לַגְּמַלִּים ends the verse.

commentary.summary: Radak: "blessed of the LORD" means that the LORD has blessed him with wealth, as Laban sees it.
Rashi: he cleared the house of idolatry, from Bereshit Rabbah; this is midrash, not the plain sense of the verb.
Radak: the house was cleared for him and his men, and a place for the camels too.
Sforno: since you asked only for a place to lodge the camels, why do you want to stand outside, you and your men?

apparatus: פִּנִּיתִי: the lexicon entry for פָּנָה lists no piʿel sense; the English takes its sense from the context.

segments.english: The man came into the house, and loosened the camels, and gave straw and fodder to the camels, and water to wash his feet and the feet of the men with him.
segments.literal: and-came the-man to-the-house and-loosened the-camels and-gave straw and-fodder to-the-camels and-water to-wash feet-his and-feet-of the-men who with-him

tokens.note: Ibn Ezra reads מִסְפּוֹא as a general word and barley in its place; the English keeps the general word

phrases.english: The man came into the house
gave straw and fodder to the camels
and water to wash his feet
and the feet of the men

phrases.literal: 'who': the relative, with no English counterpart

grammar: The wayyiqtol chain וַיָּבֹא, וַיְפַתַּח, וַיִּתֵּן keeps the order of the actions: came, loosened, gave.
וַיְפַתַּח is a piʿel: "loosened". The lexicon gives "loosen" for this sense; the object is the camels.
לִרְחֹץ is an infinitive construct after מַיִם: "water to wash".
אֲשֶׁר אִתּוֹ is a relative with אֵת: "who with him"; the English keeps "with him" without a relative verb.
The pashta on וּמִסְפּוֹא divides the gift of feed from the water; the silluq on אִתּוֹ ends the verse.
segments.note: The subject of וַיְפַתַּח and of the two following verbs is not named. The English leaves it open, as the Hebrew does. Ramban reads the subject as Laban (commentary).
context: Camels (גְּמַלִּים) are the animals of the caravan in this chapter. When camels came into use for riding and transport in this region is disputed; the English takes no side on it.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: מִסְפּוֹא is the name of the beasts' food ("שֵׁם מַאֲכַל בְּהֵמוֹת"), a general name, and barley stands in its place.
Rashi: he untied their muzzles, which stopped their mouths so that they would not graze in other fields on the way.
Ramban: the man who came is Eliezer, but the subject of "and loosened the camels" is Laban, who did this for his guests; he finds it far-fetched that Eliezer gave the water to wash his own feet.
Radak: he freed the camels from their bonds, as one frees beasts from the road; the sages' reading of the muzzles he gives as midrash.

apparatus: The subject of וַיְפַתַּח is not named; the English leaves it open.
